fields.resolution_rationale:
The dispute concerns whether the Patrick Flynn (age 5) enumerated in Thomas Flynn's 1850 Schuylkill County household is the same person as the Patrick Flynn whose 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father. Two Patrick Flynns of similar age appear in the 1850 Schuylkill County census — household 84 (age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household) and household 197 (age 6) — and the death certificate does not specify which man's son the decedent was. This matters because resolving it confirms or undermines the central conclusion that Thomas Flynn was Patrick's father.

For the Thomas Flynn household identification, three sources converge: the 1850 census places a Patrick Flynn (age 5) in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (a_001, a_002, a_004); the 1860 census independently places a Patrick Flynn (age 15, consistent with born ~1845) still in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (a_009, a_010); and the 1908 death certificate names 'Thomas Flynn' as the decedent's father, as reported by son-in-law James Brown (a_013). Brown is a secondary informant — not present at Patrick's birth — but the claim is specific and uncontradicted. The competing candidate, household 197's Patrick Flynn, shares the name and approximate age but appears in no record connected to Thomas Flynn.

The identification of the Thomas Flynn household Patrick as the 1908 decedent is the more reliable conclusion. The decisive evidence is the death certificate's affirmative naming of Thomas Flynn as father — a specific claim that directly ties the decedent to Thomas Flynn's household rather than to any other. The 1860 census corroborates independently: it places a Patrick Flynn continuously in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household a decade after 1850, making the same-county 1908 death a coherent continuation of that residence. Two independent sources agree; none contradicts them. The competing candidate has no Thomas Flynn connection in any record.

The alternative candidacy exists because of structural features of mid-nineteenth-century Irish Catholic immigration, not because of any substantive evidence pointing to household 197's Patrick. 'Patrick' was the most common Irish Catholic given name — the patron saint's name, used across generations — and 'Flynn' (anglicized Ó Floinn) was one of the most common Munster Irish surnames, often recorded as O'Flynn or Flinn (confirmed by the FamilySearch Ireland Naming Customs wiki). Same-name clustering within a single county was demographically near-inevitable. The 1850 census also recorded no relationship column, making household membership alone insufficient to establish parentage without corroborating sources. The ambiguity is a record-era artifact, resolved here by the death certificate's affirmative father-naming and the 1860 household continuity — not by the disappearance of the alternative candidate.

The researcher's careful reexamination of the same original act reads the first letter as T: 'Tannetje van Noord.' The birth act is the original record; the marriage index derives from the same underlying document and is not an independent source. The OCR reading is a machine derivative. The preponderance favors 'Tannetje van Noord'; a_002 (birth act) is the conceptually preferred assertion, but the [?] in its recorded value prevents the system from formally closing this conflict until the assertion is re-extracted with the confirmed reading.

The 'Fannetje' reading in the marriage index is explained by a derivative transcription error: in Dutch 19th-century script, capital T and F both begin with a horizontal crossbar, and copyists regularly confused them when transcribing into summary registers. The OCR 'Jannetje' is a machine misread of the same ambiguous stroke; neither the clerk's F nor the OCR's J undermines the researcher's determination that the letter is T.
